title: The Long Hunt for the Last Case
paragraphs: On May 8, 1980, the World Health Assembly, meeting in Geneva, declared that smallpox had been eradicated from the earth.
No other human disease has been deliberately driven to extinction in nature, and the achievement deserves a close look, because it was not inevitable.
The variola virus passed from person to person, usually by droplets from a sick person's nose and mouth.
After roughly twelve days of incubation came fever, then a rash that ripened into deep pustules on the face, arms, and legs.
The severe form, variola major, killed about 30 percent of the people it infected, and many survivors were left deeply scarred or blind.
In the twentieth century alone the disease killed an estimated 300 million people.

Long before anyone understood viruses, people noticed that survivors of smallpox never caught it again, and some drew a bold conclusion: a mild case given on purpose might buy lifelong protection at a bearable price.
The practice, later called variolation after variola, the Latin name of the disease, meant scratching matter from a smallpox patient's pustules into the skin of a healthy person.
It was in use in China, India, the Ottoman Empire, and parts of Africa well before Europeans adopted it.
In Boston in 1721, the minister Cotton Mather, who had learned of the practice from Onesimus, an enslaved West African man, persuaded the physician Zabdiel Boylston to try it.
About one in forty of Boylston's inoculated patients died, compared with about one in seven of the Bostonians who caught smallpox naturally.
The improvement was real, but variolation gave a person a genuine case of smallpox, and that person could pass the disease to neighbors who had not agreed to any risk.

Edward Jenner, a country physician in Gloucestershire, took the next step by testing a piece of rural folklore: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild infection of the hands, did not catch smallpox.
On May 14, 1796, he took matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inoculated an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps.
That July he variolated the boy with smallpox matter, and no disease followed.
Jenner published his findings in 1798, and the Latin word for cow, vacca, gave the procedure its name, vaccination.
He was not the first to try cowpox: a Dorset farmer named Benjamin Jesty had inoculated his wife and sons with it in 1774.
What Jenner added, and what history rightly credits him for, was a deliberate test, a written account, and years of argument for the method against ridicule.
Vaccination spread quickly across Europe and the Americas, and in 1853 England made it compulsory for infants.
By the mid twentieth century smallpox was gone from Europe and North America, yet it remained endemic across much of Asia, Africa, and South America.
In 1958 Viktor Zhdanov, a Soviet deputy health minister, proposed to the World Health Assembly that the disease be eradicated worldwide, and the Assembly agreed the following year.
The program that followed had good intentions and almost no money, and for eight years it drifted.
In 1967 the World Health Organization launched what it called the Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme, with about 2.4 million dollars a year from its own budget.
Smallpox was then endemic in more than thirty countries, with an estimated 10 to 15 million cases and some two million deaths every year.
The American epidemiologist Donald A. Henderson was sent to Geneva to direct the effort, and he led it until 1977.
Ten years, he was told, was the goal, and almost no one in public health thought it could be met.
Two pieces of technology made the field work possible.
The first was a freeze-dried vaccine, developed by Leslie Collier in London in the 1950s, that stayed potent for weeks in tropical heat without refrigeration.
The second was the bifurcated needle, invented in 1965 by Benjamin Rubin of Wyeth Laboratories, who ground the eye of a sewing needle into two prongs.
Dipped into a vial, the prongs held a single dose, and fifteen quick pricks into the skin gave a reliable vaccination with about a quarter of the vaccine older methods required.
A villager could learn to use it in minutes, and the needles could be boiled and used again.
Smallpox was also, in a sense, an easy target, and I think any honest account must say so.
The virus infected only humans, so there was no animal reservoir to bring it back.
There were no silent carriers: everyone infected developed the rash, and the rash was so distinctive that a trained searcher could spot it across a room.
A patient became infectious only around the time the rash appeared, and by then was usually too ill to travel far.
Survivors were immune for life, and their scars recorded the fact.
A disease with hidden infections or an animal host would have demanded a different campaign altogether.
The original plan was mass vaccination: reach at least 80 percent of every population and the disease should starve.
Experience in eastern Nigeria in late 1966 changed the plan.

William Foege, an American physician working there, ran short of vaccine during an outbreak, so instead of vaccinating everyone he used a missionary radio network to locate cases, isolated the patients, and vaccinated the households and villages around them.
The outbreak ended within months, with a fraction of the vaccine a blanket campaign would have consumed.

The method became known as surveillance and containment, or ring vaccination, and its logic is simple: a virus that cannot live outside people dies out when every chain of transmission runs into immune hosts.
Rather than immunize a whole country, the program drew a ring of immune people around each case and let the virus burn out inside it.
Surveillance meant finding cases, and finding cases meant persuading ordinary people to report them.
Teams carried recognition cards showing a child covered in the rash, and governments offered cash rewards for reporting a case.
In India, from 1973 to 1975, more than 100,000 health workers went house to house across the country in repeated searches.
India recorded its last case in May 1975, and the last case of variola major anywhere was a small girl, Rahima Banu, on Bhola Island in Bangladesh, that October.
The disease made its final stand in the Horn of Africa.
In October 1977 a hospital cook in Merca, Somalia, named Ali Maow Maalin caught the milder form, variola minor, after riding in a vehicle with two infected children.
He recovered, and he turned out to be the last person on earth to catch smallpox naturally.
The last death came a year later and far from any endemic zone: in 1978 Janet Parker, a medical photographer in Birmingham, England, was infected by virus from a laboratory in her building and died.
After two more years of searching turned up nothing, a global commission certified in December 1979 that the disease was gone, and the Assembly's declaration followed the next spring.
The whole program cost roughly 300 million dollars, with the endemic countries themselves paying the larger share.
Set against the savings it was one of the great bargains in medicine: countries could stop vaccinating, as the United States had done for children in 1972.
That mattered because the vaccine was not harmless and caused about one death for every million people vaccinated.
Eradication retired that risk along with the disease.
The virus itself survives in two guarded laboratories, one in Atlanta and one in Russia, and whether to destroy those stocks has been debated for decades.
It is tempting to read the campaign as a template, and I would resist that reading.

Smallpox was a vivid, slow-moving, human-only disease with a cheap and durable vaccine, and the campaigns against polio and measles, which lack some of those advantages, have found the last mile longer.

The lesson that does carry over is the one Foege stumbled on in Nigeria: that finding the disease is worth more than blanketing the population, and that a small team with good information can beat a large one without it.
Jenner predicted in 1801 that his practice would one day annihilate smallpox, and it took 179 years of unglamorous searching to prove him right.

questions.stem: According to the passage, variola major
choices: was the milder of the two forms and rarely left scars
spread mainly through contaminated water and food
was first distinguished from variola minor in 1977
produced a rash only on the trunk of the body
killed about 30 percent of the people it infected

proof.quote: The severe form, variola major, killed about 30 percent of the people it infected

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the severe form, variola major, killed about 30 percent of the people it infected and left many survivors scarred or blind.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 1 calls variola major the severe form, and paragraph 10 names variola minor as the milder one.
Wrong mechanism: paragraph 1 says the virus passed by droplets from a sick person's nose and mouth.
Outside the passage: 1977 is the year of the last natural case, not of any distinction between the two forms.
Reversed: paragraph 1 places the pustules over the face, arms, and legs.

questions.stem: According to the passage, one drawback of variolation was that
choices: it protected a person for only a few years
it required matter taken from a cow rather than a patient
an inoculated person could pass smallpox to others
it killed about one in seven of those who received it
it had never been tried outside of Europe

proof.quote: that person could pass the disease to neighbors who had not agreed to any risk

questions.why: Paragraph 2 closes by saying variolation gave a person a genuine case of smallpox, and that person could pass the disease to neighbors who had not agreed to any risk.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 2 opens with the observation that survivors never caught smallpox again, and the goal was lifelong protection.
Reversed: cowpox matter was Jenner's innovation in paragraph 3; variolation used matter from a smallpox patient.
Wrong figure: one in seven was the death rate among Bostonians who caught smallpox naturally, not among the inoculated.
Reversed: paragraph 2 says the practice was in use in China, India, the Ottoman Empire, and Africa before Europeans adopted it.

questions.stem: The author cites the Boston figures of one in forty and one in seven in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: show that variolation cut the risk of death but did not remove it
prove that Boylston was a more skilled physician than Jenner
explain why the practice originated in China and the Ottoman Empire
demonstrate that smallpox was less deadly in Boston than in London
argue that Mather should have ignored the advice of Onesimus

proof.quote: About one in forty of Boylston's inoculated patients died, compared with about one in seven
The improvement was real, but variolation gave a person a genuine case of smallpox

questions.why: The numbers in paragraph 2 are followed at once by the verdict: the improvement was real, but variolation still gave a person a genuine case of smallpox. The figures show a smaller risk, not a vanished one.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the author never compares Boylston's skill with Jenner's.
Wrong purpose: the practice's origins are stated earlier in paragraph 2 and have nothing to do with the Boston numbers.
Outside the passage: London is never mentioned, and no death rates are compared between cities.
Reversed: the figures show that Mather's borrowed idea worked, which is the opposite of a case against it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Jenner's experiment of 1796, James Phipps
choices: caught smallpox after being inoculated with cowpox
was a milkmaid who had already recovered from cowpox
was inoculated with cowpox by the farmer Benjamin Jesty
received cowpox matter and later resisted smallpox
developed a severe case of cowpox that scarred his hands

proof.quote: inoculated an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps
That July he variolated the boy with smallpox matter, and no disease followed.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Jenner inoculated the boy with matter from a cowpox sore in May 1796, then variolated him with smallpox matter that July, and no disease followed.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 3 says no disease followed the smallpox test.
Wrong person: Sarah Nelmes was the milkmaid; Phipps was an eight-year-old boy.
Wrong person: Jesty inoculated his own wife and sons in 1774, not Phipps.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the severity of the boy's cowpox or any scarring.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Benjamin Jesty receives less credit than Jenner mainly because Jesty
choices: neither tested the method on purpose nor published an account
inoculated his family with smallpox matter rather than cowpox
performed his inoculations more than twenty years after Jenner
was a physician whose work was rejected by the Royal Society
used a virus that was later shown to be unrelated to cowpox

proof.quote: What Jenner added, and what history rightly credits him for, was a deliberate test, a written account
a Dorset farmer named Benjamin Jesty had inoculated his wife and sons with it in 1774

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Jesty tried cowpox first, then names what Jenner added and is rightly credited for: a deliberate test and a written account. The step past the line is that Jesty is remembered less because he supplied neither.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 3 says Jesty inoculated his family with cowpox, not smallpox.
Reversed timing: Jesty's 1774 inoculations came 22 years before Jenner's experiment.
Wrong detail: paragraph 3 calls Jesty a farmer, and the Royal Society never appears in the passage.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the identity of the virus Jesty used, and paragraph 3 says it was cowpox.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 4, the word 'drifted' most nearly means
choices: was carried along slowly by a current of water
piled up slowly in heaps, like windblown snow
made little progress for lack of direction
moved steadily and purposefully toward its goal
was abandoned entirely by its sponsors

proof.quote: had good intentions and almost no money, and for eight years it drifted

questions.why: Paragraph 4 pairs the word with good intentions and almost no money, and the next paragraph describes the 1967 relaunch as a fresh start. A program that drifted was one that made little headway for lack of money and direction.
distractorNotes: This is the literal sense of the word, moving with a current, and nothing in the sentence involves water.
Snow and sand drift into heaps; a program does not.
Reversed: a drifting program is one that is not moving steadily toward anything.
Too strong: the program was underfunded and aimless, but the passage never says its sponsors abandoned it, and the Assembly relaunched it in 1967.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the eradication program launched in 1967 EXCEPT:
choices: It was given about 2.4 million dollars a year from the organization's own budget.
It was directed from Geneva by Donald A. Henderson.
It was launched by the World Health Organization.
It was set a goal of ten years.
It was expected by most public health experts to succeed.

proof.quote: about 2.4 million dollars a year from its own budget
sent to Geneva to direct the effort
the World Health Organization launched
Ten years, he was told, was the goal
almost no one in public health thought it could be met

questions.why: Paragraph 5 confirms the budget, the leader, the launching organization, and the ten-year goal. It also says almost no one in public health thought the goal could be met, which rules out the idea that experts expected success.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5, sentence 1 gives the figure of about 2.4 million dollars a year from the organization's own budget.
Paragraph 5, sentence 3 says Henderson was sent to Geneva to direct the effort.
Paragraph 5, sentence 1 names the World Health Organization as the launcher.
Paragraph 5, sentence 4 says ten years was the goal.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, before the freeze-dried vaccine became available, vaccination campaigns in hot climates would most likely have
choices: relied on the bifurcated needle to conserve doses
struggled to keep the vaccine potent without refrigeration
been unnecessary because smallpox was absent from the tropics
used variolation in place of vaccination
succeeded wherever the recognition cards were distributed

proof.quote: stayed potent for weeks in tropical heat without refrigeration
Two pieces of technology made the field work possible.

questions.why: Paragraph 6 presents the freeze-dried vaccine as one of two technologies that made field work possible, because it stayed potent for weeks in tropical heat without refrigeration. The step past the line is that earlier vaccine, lacking that property, would have lost potency in the heat unless it could be kept cold.
distractorNotes: Wrong timing: paragraph 6 dates the needle to 1965, after the freeze-dried vaccine, and the needle conserves doses rather than preserving them.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 says smallpox remained endemic across much of Asia, Africa, and South America.
Outside the passage: variolation is never offered as a fallback once vaccination existed.
Wrong paragraph: recognition cards in paragraph 9 helped find cases; they say nothing about keeping vaccine potent.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the bifurcated needle
choices: was developed by Leslie Collier at a laboratory in London
injected a full dose of vaccine beneath the skin in one stroke
could be used safely only by physicians with special training
needed about a quarter of the vaccine that older methods used
had to be thrown away after one use to prevent infection

proof.quote: with about a quarter of the vaccine older methods required

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says fifteen quick pricks with the bifurcated needle produced a reliable vaccination with about a quarter of the vaccine older methods required.
distractorNotes: Wrong person: Collier developed the freeze-dried vaccine; Benjamin Rubin invented the needle.
Wrong mechanism: paragraph 6 says the prongs held a dose that went in by fifteen quick pricks, not a single injection.
Reversed: paragraph 6 says a villager could learn to use it in minutes.
Reversed: paragraph 6 says the needles could be boiled and used again.

questions.stem: The author calls smallpox an easy target in paragraph 7 primarily to
choices: argue that the campaign deserved less praise than it received
qualify the achievement by noting the disease's own vulnerabilities
explain why the freeze-dried vaccine survived for weeks in tropical heat
suggest that eradication could have been finished well before 1977
introduce the recognition cards used to spot the rash

proof.quote: an easy target, and I think any honest account must say so
would have demanded a different campaign altogether

questions.why: Paragraph 7 opens in the author's own voice, insisting that an honest account admit the disease's weaknesses, then lists them. The paragraph tempers the triumph by crediting the virus's biology, not only the campaign.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author tempers the praise but never says the campaign was overpraised, and paragraph 11 calls it one of the great bargains in medicine.
Wrong paragraph: the vaccine's heat tolerance is explained in paragraph 6 and has nothing to do with the virus's biology.
Outside the passage: the author never suggests the job could have been finished sooner.
Wrong paragraph: recognition cards appear in paragraph 9, and the easy-target remark is about the disease, not the tools.

questions.stem: The passage names all of the following as features that made smallpox vulnerable to eradication EXCEPT:
choices: The virus infected only humans.
Survivors were immune for life.
A patient became infectious only around the time the rash appeared.
The rash was distinctive enough to spot at a distance.
The virus was destroyed within hours by tropical heat.

proof.quote: The virus infected only humans
Survivors were immune for life
A patient became infectious only around the time the rash appeared
the rash was so distinctive that a trained searcher could spot it across a room

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lists the human-only host, the unmistakable rash, the late onset of infectiousness, and lifelong immunity. Heat is mentioned in paragraph 6, but it is the vaccine that survives heat; nothing says the virus was destroyed by it.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 7, sentence 2 says the virus infected only humans.
Paragraph 7, sentence 5 says survivors were immune for life.
Paragraph 7, sentence 4 says a patient became infectious only around the time the rash appeared.
Paragraph 7, sentence 3 says a trained searcher could spot the rash across a room.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when William Foege ran short of vaccine in eastern Nigeria, he
choices: postponed the campaign until more vaccine arrived from Geneva
vaccinated at least 80 percent of the surrounding population
used jet injectors to stretch the remaining supply
isolated patients and vaccinated the villages around them
distributed recognition cards and offered cash rewards

proof.quote: isolated the patients, and vaccinated the households and villages around them

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says Foege used a radio network of missionaries to locate cases, isolated the patients, and vaccinated the households and villages around them.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: no delay or shipment from Geneva is mentioned; Foege acted with what he had.
Reversed: 80 percent coverage was the original mass vaccination plan that Foege's experience replaced.
Outside the passage: jet injectors are never mentioned.
Wrong paragraph: recognition cards and cash rewards belong to the surveillance methods in paragraph 9.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle of surveillance and containment described in paragraph 8?
choices: A city sprays insecticide along every street each spring to hold down mosquitoes
A fire crew clears a strip of bare ground around a blaze so it runs out of fuel
A school sends every student home for a week whenever one child has the flu
A hospital gives all of its staff a flu shot at the start of each winter
A farmer plants a different crop in each field every year to keep the soil fertile

proof.quote: drew a ring of immune people around each case and let the virus burn out inside it
dies out when every chain of transmission runs into immune hosts

questions.why: Paragraph 8's rule is to surround each outbreak with a barrier it cannot cross and let it burn out inside, rather than treating the whole population. A firebreak cleared around a blaze so the fire runs out of fuel is the same move.
distractorNotes: This is the blanket approach paragraph 8 contrasts with containment: treating every street rather than ringing an outbreak.
Wrong mechanism: sending everyone home is a shutdown of the whole group, not a ring drawn around the one case.
This is mass vaccination of everyone in advance, the original plan paragraph 8 says was replaced.
Unrelated: crop rotation protects soil fertility and involves no outbreak and no ring.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the campaign in India between 1973 and 1975
choices: relied chiefly on vaccinating 80 percent of the population
recorded the last case of variola major anywhere on earth in 1975
sent over 100,000 workers house to house in repeated searches
cost roughly 300 million dollars, paid mostly by India itself
was directed in the field by William Foege

proof.quote: more than 100,000 health workers went house to house across the country in repeated searches

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says that in India, from 1973 to 1975, more than 100,000 health workers went house to house across the country in repeated searches.
distractorNotes: Reversed: 80 percent coverage was the original mass plan in paragraph 8; the Indian campaign was a search.
Wrong country: paragraph 9 places the last case of variola major on Bhola Island in Bangladesh.
Wrong paragraph: the 300 million dollar figure in paragraph 11 is the cost of the whole global program.
Outside the passage: Foege's work is placed in eastern Nigeria in paragraph 8.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Janet Parker's death in 1978 did not undermine the claim that smallpox had been eradicated because
choices: her infection came from a laboratory, not from natural spread
she recovered, as Ali Maow Maalin had recovered the year before
her illness was the milder form, variola minor
the global commission had already certified eradication
she lived in England, where vaccination had long been compulsory

proof.quote: was infected by virus from a laboratory in her building and died
the last person on earth to catch smallpox naturally

questions.why: Paragraph 10 calls Maalin the last person to catch smallpox naturally, then describes Parker's infection as coming from a laboratory, far from any endemic zone. The step past the line is that a laboratory infection is not natural transmission, so it did not restart the count.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 10 says Parker died.
Unsupported: the passage never says which form Parker had; variola minor is attached to Maalin.
Reversed timing: the commission certified eradication in December 1979, more than a year after Parker's death in 1978.
Wrong reasoning: compulsory vaccination in England is mentioned in paragraph 4 about 1853, and the passage never links it to Parker's case.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the idea that the smallpox campaign is a template for other diseases is best described as
choices: contemptuous
admiring
cautious
indifferent
resigned

proof.quote: I would resist that reading
The lesson that does carry over

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says the author would resist reading the campaign as a template, then concedes the one lesson that does carry over. Resisting while granting a part is a cautious stance, not a hostile or an admiring one.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author resists the idea politely and still salvages a lesson from it.
Reversed: the author admires the campaign, not the idea that it is a template.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position and explains it.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 12 suggests reluctant acceptance of the idea.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Edward Jenner's cowpox experiment of 1796 made the eventual disappearance of smallpox inevitable, whatever came after it
Smallpox was ended by a long campaign in which surveillance and the virus's own biology mattered as much as the vaccine
Variolation deserves more credit than vaccination, since it protected people for centuries before Jenner was born
The methods that ended smallpox can be transferred without change to the campaigns against polio and measles
The laboratory stocks of smallpox virus in Atlanta and Russia should be destroyed before an accident releases them

proof.quote: the achievement deserves a close look, because it was not inevitable
Smallpox was also, in a sense, an easy target
finding the disease is worth more than blanketing the population

questions.why: The passage traces smallpox from variolation and Jenner through the 1967 program, then gives equal weight to the disease's own vulnerabilities in paragraph 7 and to the surveillance strategy in paragraphs 8 and 9, closing with the lesson that finding cases beats blanket coverage. Only the answer holds all of that together.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 1 says the achievement was not inevitable, and it took 179 more years of work.
Reversed: paragraph 2 ends with variolation's serious drawback, and the passage never ranks it above vaccination.
Contradicted: paragraph 12 explicitly resists reading the campaign as a template for polio and measles.
Outside the passage: paragraph 11 reports the debate over the stocks without taking a side.
